strengths: MaskSub offers a simple, technically coherent way to introduce strong masking into supervised training: an unmasked branch supplies detached targets for a masked branch sharing the same parameters. The method adds no inference overhead and integrates readily with established training recipes.

The main empirical contribution is well supported. Table 1 reports improvements across ViT-S/B/L/H and both training lengths, including gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points at 400 epochs. Results also extend to ResNet, Swin, and pretrained-model fine-tuning. Table A.12 reports ViT-B accuracy improving from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02, providing evidence beyond a single favorable run.

The paper explicitly considers computation. Table 7 reports 84.1% for ViT-B with MaskSub at 25 GPU days versus 83.7% for longer baseline training at 26 GPU days. Table 8 also shows better accuracy and lower training cost than CoSub in the evaluated setting. These comparisons support practical usefulness beyond equal-epoch improvements.

Evaluation extends meaningfully beyond ImageNet classification. Tables A.2–A.4 report improvements in ADE20K segmentation, COCO detection and instance segmentation, and distribution-shift benchmarks. For example, ViT-B ImageNet-A accuracy increases from 36.8% to 41.9%.

The appendix substantially strengthens the submission through masking-ratio and loss-weight ablations, repeated-run statistics, and detailed vision training configurations. Taken together, the practical contribution and breadth of supporting evidence favor weak acceptance.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental: the method combines existing token dropping with consistency-based self-distillation and closely relates to the cited submodel-training approaches. Table A.7 already improves the 100-epoch baseline from 77.4% to 78.4% with zero masking, versus 79.2% with 50% masking, showing that the gain is only partly attributable to masking. Furthermore, Table 6 compares different training recipes; it cannot establish the asserted incompatibility of earlier self-distillation methods with strong recipes.

The explanation of 'automatic difficulty control' exceeds the evidence. Equation 3 applies distillation to every example and contains no correctness-based selection, contrary to the statement that masking is effectively restricted to successful predictions. A confidently incorrect teacher can still impose a strong incorrect target. Figure 3's aggregate gradient norms support an interpretation of changing training dynamics, but do not establish the proposed per-example mechanism. Table A.6 also leaves unclear whether 'without KD' removes the auxiliary loss or replaces its targets with labels.

The broad improvement claims require qualification. Table A.9 shows ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy falling from 91.69% to 89.55% when MaskSub is used in both pretraining and fine-tuning. Section 4.2 explicitly states that CLIP's best checkpoint accuracy matches the baseline, so its reported gain concerns final-epoch performance. ResNet and Swin require approximately twice the training computation, and comparable-budget Swin results are absent.

Uncertainty and reproducibility coverage are uneven. Although several important experiments include three-run statistics, small gains such as the 0.1-point BEiTv2 improvements and modest GLUE improvements lack corresponding uncertainty estimates. The GLUE implementation description also omits key fine-tuning settings, limiting independent assessment of that extension.

There are correctable numerical reporting errors. Section 4.4 claims one-sixth of GradAug's training cost, whereas Table 9 reports 8.6 versus 23.4 GPU days, approximately 37% of the total cost. Table 10 labels the ViT-S Cars change from 80.9 to 92.2 as +1.3 rather than +11.3. These are presentation issues rather than grounds to dismiss the central empirical contribution.
